1 # Visual Companion Guide 2 3 Browser-based visual brainstorming companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and options. 4 5 ## When to Use 6 7 Decide per-question, not per-session. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?** 8 9 **Use the browser** when the content itself is visual: 10 11 - **UI mockups** — wireframes, layouts, navigation structures, component designs 12 - **Architecture diagrams** — system components, data flow, relationship maps 13 - **Side-by-side visual comparisons** — comparing two layouts, two color schemes, two design directions 14 - **Design polish** — when the question is about look and feel, spacing, visual hierarchy 15 - **Spatial relationships** — state machines, flowcharts, entity relationships rendered as diagrams 16 17 **Use the terminal** when the content is text or tabular: 18 19 - **Requirements and scope questions** — "what does X mean?", "which features are in scope?" 20 - **Conceptual A/B/C choices** — picking between approaches described in words 21 - **Tradeoff lists** — pros/cons, comparison tables 22 - **Technical decisions** — API design, data modeling, architectural approach selection 23 - **Clarifying questions** — anything where the answer is words, not a visual preference 24 25 A question *about* a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What kind of wizard do you want?" is conceptual — use the terminal. "Which of these wizard layouts feels right?" is visual — use the browser. 26 27 ## How It Works 28 29 The server watches a directory for HTML files and serves the newest one to the browser. You write HTML content to `screen_dir`, the user sees it in their browser and can click to select options. Selections are recorded to `state_dir/events` that you read on your next turn. 30 31 **Content fragments vs full documents:** If your HTML file starts with `/.hyperpowers/brainstorm/` for the session directory. 57 58 **Note:** Pass the project root as `--project-dir` so mockups persist in `.hyperpowers/brainstorm/` and survive server restarts. Without it, files go to `/tmp` and get cleaned up. Remind the user to add `.hyperpowers/` to `.gitignore` if it's not already there. 59 60 **Launching the server by platform:** 61 62 **Claude Code:** 63 ```bash 64 # Default mode works — the script backgrounds the server itself. 65 scripts/start-server.sh --project-dir /path/to/project --open 66 ``` 67 68 On Windows, the script auto-detects and switches to foreground mode (which blocks the tool call). Use `run_in_background: true` on the Bash tool call so the server survives across conversation turns, then read `$STATE_DIR/server-info` on the next turn to get the URL and port. 69 70 **Codex:** 71 ```bash 72 # Codex reaps background processes. The script auto-detects CODEX_CI and 73 # switches to foreground mode. Run it normally — no extra flags needed. 74 scripts/start-server.sh --project-dir /path/to/project --open 75 ``` 76 77 **Copilot CLI:** 78 ```bash 79 # Start it with Copilot CLI's non-blocking/background shell mechanism so the 80 # server survives across turns. Keep --foreground so the harness, not the 81 # script, owns backgrounding. The launcher is a .sh, so invoke it via bash 82 # (on Windows, call Git Bash's bash.exe from the PowerShell tool). 83 bash scripts/start-server.sh --project-dir /path/to/project --open --foreground 84 ``` 85 86 **Other environments:** The server must keep running in the background across conversation turns. If your environment reaps detached processes, use `--foreground` and launch the command with your platform's background execution mechanism. 87 88 If the URL is unreachable from your browser (common in remote/containerized setups), bind a non-loopback host: 89 90 ```bash 91 scripts/start-server.sh \ 92 --project-dir /path/to/project \ 93 --host 0.0.0.0 \ 94 --url-host localhost 95 ``` 96 97 Use `--url-host` to control what hostname is printed in the returned URL JSON. 98 99 ## The Loop 100 101 1. **Check server is alive**, then **write HTML** to a new file in `screen_dir`: 102 - **Required: confirm the server is alive before referring to the URL or pushing a screen.** Check that `$STATE_DIR/server-info` exists and `$STATE_DIR/server-stopped` does not. If it has shut down, restart it with `start-server.sh` using the **same `--project-dir`** — it reuses the same port, so the user's open tab reconnects on its own (it shows a "paused" overlay while the server is down) and you don't need to send a new URL. The server auto-exits after 4 hours idle (configurable with `--idle-timeout-minutes`). 103 - Use semantic filenames: `platform.html`, `visual-style.html`, `layout.html` 104 - **Never reuse filenames** — each screen gets a fresh file 105 - Use your file-creation tool — **never use cat/heredoc** (dumps noise into terminal) 106 - Server automatically serves the newest file 107 108 2. **Tell user what to expect and end your turn:** 109 - Remind them of the URL (every step, not just first) 110 - Give a brief text summary of what's on screen (e.g., "Showing 3 layout options for the homepage") 111 - Ask them to respond in the terminal: "Take a look and let me know what you think. Click to select an option if you'd like." 112 113 3. **On your next turn** — after the user responds in the terminal: 114 - Read `$STATE_DIR/events` if it exists — this contains the user's browser interactions (clicks, selections) as JSON lines 115 - Merge with the user's terminal text to get the full picture 116 - The terminal message is the primary feedback; `state_dir/events` provides structured interaction data 117 118 4. **Iterate or advance** — if feedback changes current screen, write a new file (e.g., `layout-v2.html`). Only move to the next question when the current step is validated. 119 120 5. **Unload when returning to terminal** — when the next step doesn't need the browser (e.g., a clarifying question, a tradeoff discussion), push a waiting screen to clear the stale content: 121 122 ```html 123 124
125

Continuing in terminal...

126
127 ``` 128 129 This prevents the user from staring at a resolved choice while the conversation has moved on. When the next visual question comes up, push a new content file as usual. 130 131 6. Repeat until done. 132 133 ## Writing Content Fragments 134 135 Write just the content that goes inside the page. The server wraps it in the frame template automatically (header, theme CSS, connection status, and all interactive infrastructure). 136 137 **Minimal example:** 138 139 ```html 140

Which layout works better?

1	---
2	name: brainstorming
3	description: "You MUST use this before any creative work - creating features, building components, adding functionality, or modifying behavior. Explores user intent, requirements and design before implementation."
4	---
5	
6	# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs
7	
8	Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.
9	
10	Start by classifying how much process the request needs, then work
11	through your path: understand the context, refine the idea, present a
12	design, and get your human partner's approval.
13	
14	<HARD-GATE>
15	Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any
16	project, or take any implementation action until you have told your
17	human partner what you intend and they have approved it. This applies
18	to EVERY task on EVERY path below — the ceremony scales with the task;
19	the approval gate never does.
20	</HARD-GATE>
21	
22	**REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use hyperpowers:communication for everything your human partner reads on every path: the questions, the approach comparison, the design presentation, and the spec.
23	
24	**After every context compaction:** Claude Code re-attaches this skill cut to its first 20,000 characters, which ends before the spec-writing steps, and a full Read you made before the compaction does not survive it. After each compaction, the first and every later one, Read this file in full before your next action (a question to your human partner, a visual-companion step, or writing the spec), along with any other skill you are following whose re-attached copy is cut short.
25	
26	## Three Paths
27	
28	Before your first question, classify the request and say the
29	classification out loud — "this looks bounded, so I'll present a short
30	design here rather than write a spec" — so your human partner can
31	override it:
32	
33	- **Spike** — a feasibility question ("can we...", "is it possible...",
34	  "quick and dirty is fine") whose output is an answer, not code you
35	  keep. Present the question and what you'll try in 2-3 sentences, get
36	  a nod, then find out as cheaply as correctness allows. No design
37	  doc, no spec file. Report findings as a recommendation; anything you
38	  built stays labeled throwaway.
39	- **Bounded** — a well-scoped change to code that already exists in
40	  this repo: a new flag, a small endpoint, a one-file fix.
41	  Understanding the kind of app is not enough — bounded means the flow
42	  you are changing is already here to read. If there is no existing
43	  flow to change, the task is not bounded. Classify by the outcome the
44	  request names, not by the code your first edit would touch: if the
45	  request names structure this repo does not have — a new module or
46	  layer, a new subsystem such as logging or storage, reuse across
47	  components that do not exist yet — the flow you would be changing is
48	  not already here, however small the first edit looks, and the task
49	  is architectural. Choosing between algorithms or options inside a
50	  function that already exists names no new structure and stays
51	  bounded. Ask the clarifying questions that matter, present a short
52	  design IN CHAT (a few sentences to a few short paragraphs), and
53	  STOP. Implementation starts only after your human partner says yes
54	  to that design — a bounded task's approval is as hard a gate as an
55	  architectural one. No spec file, no implementation plan document.
56	- **Architectural** — new projects, new subsystems, changes that
57	  restructure how components fit together or alter interfaces others
58	  depend on. Follow the full process: questions, approaches, sectioned
59	  design, written spec, then the writing-plans skill.
60	
61	When in doubt between two paths, take the heavier one. The ratchet is
62	one-way: hidden complexity discovered mid-task upgrades the path —
63	stop, say so, and step up. Nothing downgrades mid-task.
64	
65	## Anti-Pattern: "Too Simple To Need Approval"
66	
67	Every path ends with your human partner approving your intent before
68	implementation. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config
69	change — the design may be two sentences in chat, but you MUST present
70	it and get approval. "Simple" tasks are where unexamined assumptions
71	cause the most wasted work. What scales with simplicity is the
72	artifact, never the approval.
73	
74	## Red Flags
75	
76	| Thought | Reality |
77	|---------|---------|
78	| "This is too simple to need a design" | Simple means a short design, not no design. Two sentences in chat, then approval. |
79	| "I'll call it bounded and skip the spec" | Reaching for a label to skip work IS the doubt — take the heavier path. |
80	| "It's bounded and the design is obvious — I'll start while they read it" | The gate is the approval, not the design's length. Present, then stop until you hear yes. |
81	| "I understand this kind of app, so it's bounded" | Bounded measures the repo, not your familiarity. A new project has no existing flow — it is architectural. |
82	| "The code I'd touch is right here, so it's bounded" | Bounded measures the outcome's shape, not the entry point. A request naming a new module, a new subsystem, or reuse across components that do not exist yet is architectural even when the edit starts in one file. |
83	| "The spike works, so I'll keep the code" | A spike's output is an answer. Keeping the code is a new request — classify it. |
84	| "It grew, but I'm almost done — no need to re-classify" | Hidden complexity upgrades the path mid-task. Stop and say so. |
85	| "They approved the spike, so the follow-up change is approved too" | Each task gets its own classification and its own approval. |
86	| "It's bounded, so the visual companion doesn't apply" | The companion keys on the question being visual, not on the path being heavy. Open it — the task stays bounded. |

88	## Checklist
89	
90	Classify first, announce the path, then create a task for each item on
91	your path and complete them in order.
92	
93	**Spike:**
94	1. **Explore project context** — enough to frame the probe
95	2. **Present question + probe plan** — 2-3 sentences
96	3. **Get approval** — a nod is enough
97	4. **Investigate** — as cheaply as correctness allows (The approach gate's any-path trigger applies here too — explicit request or genuinely material alternatives fire it; feasibility probes rarely do.)
98	5. **Report findings** — a recommendation; label anything built as throwaway
99	
100	**Bounded:**
101	1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
102	2. **Visual companion (conditional)** — if a question here would genuinely be clearer shown than described (a layout, a diagram, side-by-side options), open it just-in-time. Ceremony does not escalate: the design still lands in chat. See the Visual Companion section below.
103	3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, the ones that matter
104	4. **Codex approach gate (conditional)** — if the design space has real architectural, algorithmic, or data-model alternatives, or your human partner asks for Codex input, run [codex-approach-gate.md](codex-approach-gate.md) and fold its approaches into the short in-chat design with provenance tags. Ceremony does not escalate. Trivial/mechanical bounded tasks skip this silently.
105	5. **Present short design in chat** — approach, files touched, testing
106	6. **Get approval** — STOP and wait for an explicit yes; presenting the design and starting in the same breath is skipping the gate
107	7. **Implement** — proceed with the normal development workflow (TDD applies); no plan document
108	
109	**Architectural:**
110	1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
111	2. **Use the visual companion just-in-time** — NOT upfront. The first time a question would genuinely be clearer shown than described, open it then and tell the user what you're doing — no separate approval gate. If no visual question ever arises, never open it. See the Visual Companion section below.
112	3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
113	4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation. Before finalizing them, run [codex-approach-gate.md](codex-approach-gate.md) if the approach gate fires (rule below) and fold its approaches into this step with provenance tags.
114	5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
115	6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/hyperpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` (do not commit unless the user asks)
116	7. **Spec self-review** — quick inline check for placeholders, contradictions, ambiguity, scope (see below)
117	8. **Codex spec review gate** (Claude Code only) — run the Codex review gate over the spec before involving the user (see below)
118	9. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
119	10. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan
120	
121	**Codex approach gate (conditional, Claude Code only):** the gate's trigger is
122	path-independent — real architectural, algorithmic, or data-model
123	alternatives, or your human partner asking for Codex input, fire it on any
124	path. On the bounded path its approaches fold into the short in-chat design;
125	ceremony does not escalate. On the spike path it does not normally fire
126	(feasibility probes rarely present committed design alternatives), but an
127	explicit request or genuinely material alternatives still fire it.
128	Trivial/mechanical tasks skip it silently.
129	
130	**Visual companion (conditional, any path):** its trigger is path-independent
131	too — the first time a question would genuinely be clearer shown than
132	described, open it, whichever path you are on. Adding or moving something on a
133	page or screen always raises one: where it goes. Show the placements in the
134	companion before you present the design. Classification does not gate it:
135	a bounded task that opens the companion is still bounded and still ends in a
136	short in-chat design, and a spike that sketches one screen is still a spike.
137	What fires it is the question being visual, not the path being heavy. If no
138	visual question ever arises, never open it.

202	
203	## The Process
204	
205	The subsections below serve the bounded and architectural paths (a
206	spike stops at "present the probe, get a nod"). Sections from
207	**Exploring approaches** onward are architectural-path depth — for
208	bounded work, context plus a few questions plus a short in-chat design
209	is the whole process.
210	
211	**Understanding the idea:**
212	
213	- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
214	- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
215	- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
216	- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
217	- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too. When the options differ in what happens afterward, the comparison goes in chat before you ask — see Deciding Together below
218	- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
219	- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria
220	
221	**Exploring approaches:**
222	
223	- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
224	- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
225	- Lead with your recommended option and explain why
226	- YAGNI ruthlessly - remove unnecessary features from every approach and design
227	- **Codex approach gate (conditional):** when the design space has real architectural, algorithmic, or data-model alternatives — or your human partner explicitly asks — get Codex's independent approaches first via [codex-approach-gate.md](codex-approach-gate.md): blind handoff, one shot, approaches folded into this step with provenance tags and judged on merits, not origin.
228	
229	**Presenting the design:**
230	
231	- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
232	- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
233	- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
234	- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
235	- For a new project (or one with no configured tooling), the design presentation includes a short tooling question alongside the architecture: which of these to set up from the start — cheapest before any code exists: aggressive linting + auto-formatting (the stack's standard, e.g. ruff+format / eslint+prettier / clippy+rustfmt); unit-test infrastructure (runner, layout, a first passing fixture); end-to-end test infrastructure; fuzz or mutation testing where the stack supports it. The user's selections land in the spec's Global Constraints so every later plan and task inherits them.
236	- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense
237	
238	**Design for isolation and clarity:**
239	
240	- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
241	- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
242	- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
243	- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.
244	
245	**Working in existing codebases:**
246	
247	- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
248	- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
249	- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.
250	
251	## Deciding Together
252	
253	Five-word labels with a line of description each are plenty for "which of
254	these do you prefer" and nowhere near enough for a choice your human partner
255	has to live with. Whenever the options differ in what happens afterward — an
256	interface, a stored format, a default, a dependency, work that would have to
257	be redone — the comparison goes in chat, before you ask.
258	
259	That message has three parts, in this order:
260	
261	1. **The fork**, in one sentence: what actually differs between the options,
262	   not what they are named.
263	2. **One line per option**: what it buys, what it costs, and what it rules
264	   out later. Say which choices are cheap to change afterward and which are
265	   not.
266	3. **Your recommendation**, and the reason you hold it.
267	
268	Send that message. Then ask with the normal selection widget — short labels,
269	one line of description each, your recommended option first. The message is
270	how they decide; the widget is how they answer. You send both, and you fold
271	neither into the other.
272	
273	If the options differ only in what they are called — a name, an ordering, a
274	wording — ask directly. There is nothing to compare.
275	
276	## Visual Companion
277	
278	A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode, and not a path. Having it open means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.
279	
280	**Using the companion (just-in-time):** Do NOT open it upfront. Wait until a question would genuinely be clearer shown than told — a real mockup / layout / diagram question, not merely a UI *topic*. The first time that happens, just use it: start the server with `--open` so the user's browser opens to the first screen, and tell them what you're doing in the same message — no separate approval gate.
281	> "I'll sketch this in a browser tab so it's easier to see — opening it now at <URL>. (It's token-intensive, so say the word if you'd rather keep things in the terminal.)"
282	
283	If a visual question never arises, never open it. If the user asks to stop using it, continue text-only and don't reopen it unless they raise it again.
284	
285	**Per-question decision:** Even with the companion open, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**
286	
287	- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
288	- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions
289	
290	A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.
291	
292	Before opening the companion for the first time, read the detailed guide:
293	`skills/brainstorming/visual-companion.md`
294	
295	## After the Design (architectural path)
296	
297	**Documentation:**
298	
299	- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/hyperpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
300	  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
301	- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
302	- Do NOT commit the design document. Leave it as an uncommitted working file unless the user explicitly asks you to commit it.
303	- Where the design rests on something nobody confirmed, write it as
304	  `Assumption: <what>, validate via <method>` rather than as a fact; the
305	  plan will attach the deadline. The placeholder scan accepts that form
306	  and flags bare TBD or TODO.
307	
308	**Spec Self-Review:**
309	After writing the spec document, look at it with fresh eyes:
310	
311	1. **Placeholder scan:** Any "TBD", "TODO", incomplete sections, or vague requirements? Fix them.
312	2. **Internal consistency:** Do any sections contradict each other? Does the architecture match the feature descriptions?
313	3. **Scope check:** Is this focused enough for a single implementation plan, or does it need decomposition?
314	4. **Ambiguity check:** Could any requirement be interpreted two different ways? If so, pick one and make it explicit.
315	
316	Fix any issues inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on.
317	
318	**Codex Spec Review Gate (Claude Code only):**
319	After the spec self-review passes and before involving the user, run the Codex
320	review gate over the spec file as a **document** review using the spec recipe.
321	Follow
322	[../requesting-code-review/codex-review-gate.md](../requesting-code-review/codex-review-gate.md):
323	probe availability, and if Codex is present, provide the spec path plus any
324	available approved-design context, have it review the spec, and resolve blocking
325	findings in the convergence fix loop (document-gate backstop of 4 rounds) before
326	the user review; if Codex is absent, emit the no-Codex notice and proceed. This
327	gate never blocks the user review — at worst it is skipped.
328	
329	**User Review Gate:**
330	After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:
331	
332	> "Spec written to `<path>` (not committed). Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."
333	
334	Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.
335	
336	**Implementation:**
337	
338	- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
339	- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.

steps.message:
This looks bounded: it's a change to one page that already exists. So I'll put a short design here in chat rather than write a spec, and I'll wait for your yes before I change anything.

The first question is where the filters go on the page, and that's easier to judge by looking. I'll sketch this in a browser tab so it's easier to see. I'm opening it now at http://localhost:59649/?key=21eb0c17b780a87ff2badecfa3290b84d851577b183f12d05a9dfd822b9ea38d (it uses a lot of tokens, so say so if you'd rather stay in the terminal).

Each of the three sketches has the same controls: event type, a date range, a search box, and a one-click "Failed sign-ins" shortcut. That shortcut is there because the only support tickets so far came from people looking for a failed sign-in they didn't recognize. The three sketches differ only in where those controls sit:

- **A: Filter bar above the table.** Every control is visible at once, and the bar stacks on narrow screens.
- **B: A "Filter" button that opens a popover.** Active filters show as removable tags above the table. It takes the least space, but the filters are hidden until you open it.
- **C: A side panel on desktop, stacked above the table on mobile.** The filters are always visible, but the panel takes width from a table that already has six columns.

I lean toward A. There are only four controls, so hiding them in a popover saves little, and a side panel would squeeze the table. Click one in the browser if you like, then reply here.

The companion writes its files to `.hyperpowers/` in the repo root. There's no `.gitignore` yet, so add `.hyperpowers/` to one if you want to keep it out of git. I won't commit it either way.
The filter bar above the table looks right — go with A.

Should this branch fix that, or only make sure the new filter bar doesn't make it worse?"="Leave it (Recommended)". You can now continue with these answers in mind.

steps.message:
The no-JS gap stays a follow-up. Here's the design.

**What it does.** A filter bar sits between the intro and the table and has four controls. All of them filter as you change them, and nothing submits or navigates:
- **Event type:** a Select with "All events" plus the nine existing types.
- **From and To:** two date inputs, limited to the 90 days in the data. If To is before From, the catalog message "The end date must be after the start date." shows on blur.
- **Search:** matches device, location, IP, and details. It's `type=search` with autocomplete off, a clear button, and Escape to clear.
- **"Show failed sign-ins":** a button that sets Event type to "Sign-in failed".

Filters combine, so an event must match all of them to show. A "Clear filters" button resets everything. A polite live region announces "Showing 12 of 50 events" without moving focus. When nothing matches, the table hides and an empty state appears: "No matching events" with "Try a different event type, date range, or search." The bar has the `hidden` attribute in the HTML and `activity.js` removes it, so a no-JS visitor never sees dead controls. Labels sit above the controls, and the bar wraps to a single column at 320px. I'm leaving out date presets, the time zone label, and the date format fix. Those stay follow-ups.

**Files.** All edits are to existing files; none are renamed or added:
- `public/activity.html`: the filter form, the status line, and the empty state.
- `public/activity.css`: a `:root` block with the tokens it uses, copied from 01, then the filter bar styles in tokens only. No raw hex, px, or duration values in the new lines.
- `public/activity.js`: builds rows once, then shows or hides them on filter change.

I estimate about 180 lines in total, as one `feat:` commit. I'll show you the full diff before committing and won't push.

**Testing.** The repo has no test runner, and adding one would be a new dev dependency, so I'm not adding automated tests. Instead:
- I'll grep the diff for raw hex, px, and durations.
- I'll open `activity.html` directly in Safari and Firefox and try each event type, the failed sign-ins button, a reversed date range, search with Escape, Clear filters, and a no-match search to get the empty state.
- I'll tab through the whole bar with the keyboard only and check the layout at 320px wide.
- I'll reload with JS disabled and confirm the bar stays hidden.
- I'll check that VoiceOver in Safari announces the count.

Afterward I'll tell you exactly what I clicked in each browser.

Shall I go ahead with this?

Post-compaction rule: re-read `/Users/johnss51/Development/agents/hyperpowers/.worktrees/cost-6-16-2/skills/brainstorming/SKILL.md` in full before the next action. 2. Key Technical Concepts: - The page is static HTML, CSS, and JS with no build step and no test runner. Adding a test runner would be a new dev dependency, so none is added. - Data source: `window.ACTIVITY_EVENTS` in public/activity-data.js. - Fields: `when`, `type`, `device`, `location`, `ip`, `detail`. - `when` values are UTC ISO strings like '2026-09-28T17:42Z'. - IPs are already masked, like '203.0.113.x'. - Events are newest first, about 50 of them, dated Sept 2026. - The nine event types are: Sign-in, Sign-in failed, Sign-out, Session expired, Password changed, Two-factor enabled, Email change requested, Settings updated, API token used. - No shared token sheet exists in the repo. The user chose to declare the needed tokens in a `:root` block at the top of activity.css, with a comment citing docs/ui-guidelines/01-foundations.md as the source. New rules must use only those variables, with no raw hex, px, or durations outside that `:root` block. - The no-JS empty-table gap stays a follow-up. The filter bar ships with the `hidden` attribute and JS removes it. - Guideline points that apply: - Select for 6 or more options. - Labels sit above controls in `--type-label` with a `--space-4` gap. - Search field: type=search, enterkeyhint=search, autocomplete=off, a clear button, and Escape clears it. - Date range: two sm date pickers, validated on blur. Account activity

Every sign-in and account change from the last 90 days, newest first.

When Event Device Location IP Details
``` - public/activity.js, current content: ```js // Renders every event as one table row, in API order. const tbody = document.querySelector('#activity-table tbody'); for (const event of window.ACTIVITY_EVENTS) { const row = document.createElement('tr'); for (const value of [ new Date(event.when).toLocaleString(), event.type, event.device, event.location, event.ip, event.detail, ]) { const cell = document.createElement('td'); cell.textContent = value; row.appendChild(cell); } tbody.appendChild(row); } ``` - public/activity.css, current content. Leave its existing raw values alone; retokenizing was not chosen. ```css body { font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; margin: 0; background: #f6f7f9; } .activity { max-width: 960px; margin: 3rem auto; padding: 2rem; background: #fff; border-radius: 8px; } .activity h1 { margin-top: 0; font-size: 1.5rem; } #activity-table { width: 100%; border-collapse: collapse; } #activity-table th, #activity-table td { text-align: left; padding: 0.5rem; border-bottom: 1px solid #e3e5e8; } ``` The real file is multi-line, one declaration per line. - Companion files, not to be committed: - .hyperpowers/brainstorm/2512-1793835302/content/filter-placement.html - .hyperpowers/brainstorm/2512-1793835302/content/waiting.html - The repo root has no .gitignore. Enter must not submit (preventDefault on the form's submit). - A polite live region (role=status) reads "Showing X of Y events". - When nothing matches, the table hides and an empty state shows the title "No matching events" and the body "Try a different event type, date range, or search." - Out of scope: date presets, the time zone label, and the date format fix. - JS builds the rows once, then shows or hides them. - Estimated about 180 lines, as one `feat:` commit. 6. All user messages: - "The account activity page is one long table of events and nobody can find anything in it. Add a way to narrow it down." - "The filter bar above the table looks right — go with A." - Answered the selection widget for token source: "Declare in activity.css". - Answered the selection widget for the no-JS gap: "Leave it (Recommended)". - "Yes, go ahead." - Standing NOTES.md rules, verbatim and in force: - "Show me the full diff before any commit. Never push. Never force-push. Never rewrite history on a shared branch." - "One change per commit, conventional prefixes. If a change needs two kinds of prefix it is two commits." - "Do not touch `public/legacy/` or anything under `vendor/` even if it looks dead. Ops still serves the legacy pages to two enterprise tenants." - "Keep every page readable with JavaScript disabled. Interactive extras may require JS; the content may not." - "No new runtime dependencies. Dev dependencies need a one-line justification in the commit body." - "If a test is flaky, say so and show me the run. Do not retry until green and call it fixed." - "When you are unsure whether something is in scope, ask me before doing it, not after." - "Status lines between steps, short. No emojis anywhere." - "Do not paste secrets into chat, commits, or test fixtures. The API token values on the settings page are real in staging; use the placeholder `tok_test_000` anywhere you need one." - "The reviewers are strict about the UI guidelines. A review comment about a raw hex value or a hard-coded px size costs a full review round, so check before you hand anything over." - "Never show a full IP address anywhere in the UI, logs, or screenshots. The API already masks the last octet; do not try to recover it." - "Times are stored in UTC and shown in the viewer's time zone. Never show a bare UTC time without saying so." - "Do not add analytics, tracking pixels, or third-party scripts to any page, including for debugging. Legal reviews every outbound request." - "Keep the diff small enough to review in one sitting. If it grows past about 300 lines, stop and tell me how you would split it." - "Run the page in a real browser before you say it works, and tell me which browser and what you clicked." - "Do not rename files or move them between directories unless the task is about that. Ops' nginx config points at exact paths." - "Write commit bodies for the reviewer who was not in the room: what changed, why, and what you checked." - Other NOTES points: - Do not reopen the API decisions. - Do not touch the settings page. - No CSV or export. 1	---
2	name: brainstorming
3	description: "You MUST use this before any creative work - creating features, building components, adding functionality, or modifying behavior. Explores user intent, requirements and design before implementation."
4	---
5	
6	# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs
7	
8	Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.
9	
10	Start by classifying how much process the request needs, then work
11	through your path: understand the context, refine the idea, present a
12	design, and get your human partner's approval.
13	
14	<HARD-GATE>
15	Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any
16	project, or take any implementation action until you have told your
17	human partner what you intend and they have approved it. This applies
18	to EVERY task on EVERY path below — the ceremony scales with the task;
19	the approval gate never does.
20	</HARD-GATE>
21	
22	**REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use hyperpowers:communication for everything your human partner reads on every path: the questions, the approach comparison, the design presentation, and the spec.
23	
24	**After every context compaction:** Claude Code re-attaches this skill cut to its first 20,000 characters, which ends before the spec-writing steps, and a full Read you made before the compaction does not survive it. After each compaction, the first and every later one, Read this file in full before your next action (a question to your human partner, a visual-companion step, or writing the spec), along with any other skill you are following whose re-attached copy is cut short.
25	
26	## Three Paths
27	
28	Before your first question, classify the request and say the
29	classification out loud — "this looks bounded, so I'll present a short
30	design here rather than write a spec" — so your human partner can
31	override it:
32	
33	- **Spike** — a feasibility question ("can we...", "is it possible...",
34	  "quick and dirty is fine") whose output is an answer, not code you
35	  keep. Present the question and what you'll try in 2-3 sentences, get
36	  a nod, then find out as cheaply as correctness allows. No design
37	  doc, no spec file. Report findings as a recommendation; anything you
38	  built stays labeled throwaway.
39	- **Bounded** — a well-scoped change to code that already exists in
40	  this repo: a new flag, a small endpoint, a one-file fix.
41	  Understanding the kind of app is not enough — bounded means the flow
42	  you are changing is already here to read. If there is no existing
43	  flow to change, the task is not bounded. Classify by the outcome the
44	  request names, not by the code your first edit would touch: if the
45	  request names structure this repo does not have — a new module or
46	  layer, a new subsystem such as logging or storage, reuse across
47	  components that do not exist yet — the flow you would be changing is
48	  not already here, however small the first edit looks, and the task
49	  is architectural. Choosing between algorithms or options inside a
50	  function that already exists names no new structure and stays
51	  bounded. Ask the clarifying questions that matter, present a short
52	  design IN CHAT (a few sentences to a few short paragraphs), and
53	  STOP. Implementation starts only after your human partner says yes
54	  to that design — a bounded task's approval is as hard a gate as an
55	  architectural one. No spec file, no implementation plan document.
56	- **Architectural** — new projects, new subsystems, changes that
57	  restructure how components fit together or alter interfaces others
58	  depend on. Follow the full process: questions, approaches, sectioned
59	  design, written spec, then the writing-plans skill.
60	
61	When in doubt between two paths, take the heavier one. The ratchet is
62	one-way: hidden complexity discovered mid-task upgrades the path —
63	stop, say so, and step up. Nothing downgrades mid-task.
64	
65	## Anti-Pattern: "Too Simple To Need Approval"
66	
67	Every path ends with your human partner approving your intent before
68	implementation. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config
69	change — the design may be two sentences in chat, but you MUST present
70	it and get approval. "Simple" tasks are where unexamined assumptions
71	cause the most wasted work. What scales with simplicity is the
72	artifact, never the approval.
73	
74	## Red Flags
75	
76	| Thought | Reality |
77	|---------|---------|
78	| "This is too simple to need a design" | Simple means a short design, not no design. Two sentences in chat, then approval. |
79	| "I'll call it bounded and skip the spec" | Reaching for a label to skip work IS the doubt — take the heavier path. |
80	| "It's bounded and the design is obvious — I'll start while they read it" | The gate is the approval, not the design's length. Present, then stop until you hear yes. |
81	| "I understand this kind of app, so it's bounded" | Bounded measures the repo, not your familiarity. A new project has no existing flow — it is architectural. |
82	| "The code I'd touch is right here, so it's bounded" | Bounded measures the outcome's shape, not the entry point. A request naming a new module, a new subsystem, or reuse across components that do not exist yet is architectural even when the edit starts in one file. |
83	| "The spike works, so I'll keep the code" | A spike's output is an answer. Keeping the code is a new request — classify it. |
84	| "It grew, but I'm almost done — no need to re-classify" | Hidden complexity upgrades the path mid-task. Stop and say so. |
85	| "They approved the spike, so the follow-up change is approved too" | Each task gets its own classification and its own approval. |
86	| "It's bounded, so the visual companion doesn't apply" | The companion keys on the question being visual, not on the path being heavy. Open it — the task stays bounded. |
87	
88	## Checklist
89	
90	Classify first, announce the path, then create a task for each item on
91	your path and complete them in order.
92	
93	**Spike:**
94	1. **Explore project context** — enough to frame the probe
95	2. **Present question + probe plan** — 2-3 sentences
96	3. **Get approval** — a nod is enough
97	4. **Investigate** — as cheaply as correctness allows (The approach gate's any-path trigger applies here too — explicit request or genuinely material alternatives fire it; feasibility probes rarely do.)
98	5. **Report findings** — a recommendation; label anything built as throwaway
99	
100	**Bounded:**
101	1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
102	2. **Visual companion (conditional)** — if a question here would genuinely be clearer shown than described (a layout, a diagram, side-by-side options), open it just-in-time. Ceremony does not escalate: the design still lands in chat. See the Visual Companion section below.
103	3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, the ones that matter
104	4. **Codex approach gate (conditional)** — if the design space has real architectural, algorithmic, or data-model alternatives, or your human partner asks for Codex input, run [codex-approach-gate.md](codex-approach-gate.md) and fold its approaches into the short in-chat design with provenance tags. Ceremony does not escalate. Trivial/mechanical bounded tasks skip this silently.
105	5. **Present short design in chat** — approach, files touched, testing
106	6. **Get approval** — STOP and wait for an explicit yes; presenting the design and starting in the same breath is skipping the gate
107	7. **Implement** — proceed with the normal development workflow (TDD applies); no plan document
108	
109	**Architectural:**
110	1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
111	2. **Use the visual companion just-in-time** — NOT upfront. The first time a question would genuinely be clearer shown than described, open it then and tell the user what you're doing — no separate approval gate. If no visual question ever arises, never open it. See the Visual Companion section below.
112	3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
113	4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation. Before finalizing them, run [codex-approach-gate.md](codex-approach-gate.md) if the approach gate fires (rule below) and fold its approaches into this step with provenance tags.
114	5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
115	6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/hyperpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` (do not commit unless the user asks)
116	7. **Spec self-review** — quick inline check for placeholders, contradictions, ambiguity, scope (see below)
117	8. **Codex spec review gate** (Claude Code only) — run the Codex review gate over the spec before involving the user (see below)
118	9. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
119	10. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan
120	
121	**Codex approach gate (conditional, Claude Code only):** the gate's trigger is
122	path-independent — real architectural, algorithmic, or data-model
123	alternatives, or your human partner asking for Codex input, fire it on any
124	path. On the bounded path its approaches fold into the short in-chat design;
125	ceremony does not escalate. On the spike path it does not normally fire
126	(feasibility probes rarely present committed design alternatives), but an
127	explicit request or genuinely material alternatives still fire it.
128	Trivial/mechanical tasks skip it silently.
129	
130	**Visual companion (conditional, any path):** its trigger is path-independent
131	too — the first time a question would genuinely be clearer shown than
132	described, open it, whichever path you are on. Adding or moving something on a
133	page or screen always raises one: where it goes. Show the placements in the
134	companion before you present the design. Classification does not gate it:
135	a bounded task that opens the companion is still bounded and still ends in a
136	short in-chat design, and a spike that sketches one screen is still a spike.
137	What fires it is the question being visual, not the path being heavy. If no
138	visual question ever arises, never open it.
139

195	
196	**Terminal states are path-bound.** Architectural: the ONLY skill you
197	invoke after brainstorming is writing-plans — never frontend-design,
198	mcp-builder, or any other implementation skill. Bounded: after
199	approval, implementation proceeds directly through the normal
200	development workflow; no plan document. Spike: the terminal state is a
201	reported recommendation.
202	
203	## The Process
204	
205	The subsections below serve the bounded and architectural paths (a
206	spike stops at "present the probe, get a nod"). Sections from
207	**Exploring approaches** onward are architectural-path depth — for
208	bounded work, context plus a few questions plus a short in-chat design
209	is the whole process.
210	
211	**Understanding the idea:**
212	
213	- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
214	- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
215	- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
216	- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
217	- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too. When the options differ in what happens afterward, the comparison goes in chat before you ask — see Deciding Together below
218	- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
219	- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria
220	
221	**Exploring approaches:**
222	
223	- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
224	- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
225	- Lead with your recommended option and explain why
226	- YAGNI ruthlessly - remove unnecessary features from every approach and design
227	- **Codex approach gate (conditional):** when the design space has real architectural, algorithmic, or data-model alternatives — or your human partner explicitly asks — get Codex's independent approaches first via [codex-approach-gate.md](codex-approach-gate.md): blind handoff, one shot, approaches folded into this step with provenance tags and judged on merits, not origin.
228	
229	**Presenting the design:**
230	
231	- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
232	- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
233	- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
234	- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
235	- For a new project (or one with no configured tooling), the design presentation includes a short tooling question alongside the architecture: which of these to set up from the start — cheapest before any code exists: aggressive linting + auto-formatting (the stack's standard, e.g. ruff+format / eslint+prettier / clippy+rustfmt); unit-test infrastructure (runner, layout, a first passing fixture); end-to-end test infrastructure; fuzz or mutation testing where the stack supports it. The user's selections land in the spec's Global Constraints so every later plan and task inherits them.
236	- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense
237	
238	**Design for isolation and clarity:**
239	
240	- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
241	- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
242	- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
243	- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.
244	
245	**Working in existing codebases:**
246	
247	- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
248	- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
249	- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.
250	
251	## Deciding Together
252	
253	Five-word labels with a line of description each are plenty for "which of
254	these do you prefer" and nowhere near enough for a choice your human partner
255	has to live with. Whenever the options differ in what happens afterward — an
256	interface, a stored format, a default, a dependency, work that would have to
257	be redone — the comparison goes in chat, before you ask.
258	
259	That message has three parts, in this order:
260	
261	1. **The fork**, in one sentence: what actually differs between the options,
262	   not what they are named.
263	2. **One line per option**: what it buys, what it costs, and what it rules
264	   out later. Say which choices are cheap to change afterward and which are
265	   not.
266	3. **Your recommendation**, and the reason you hold it.
267	
268	Send that message. Then ask with the normal selection widget — short labels,
269	one line of description each, your recommended option first. The message is
270	how they decide; the widget is how they answer. You send both, and you fold
271	neither into the other.
272	
273	If the options differ only in what they are called — a name, an ordering, a
274	wording — ask directly. There is nothing to compare.
275	
276	## Visual Companion
277	
278	A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode, and not a path. Having it open means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.
279	
280	**Using the companion (just-in-time):** Do NOT open it upfront. Wait until a question would genuinely be clearer shown than told — a real mockup / layout / diagram question, not merely a UI *topic*. The first time that happens, just use it: start the server with `--open` so the user's browser opens to the first screen, and tell them what you're doing in the same message — no separate approval gate.
281	> "I'll sketch this in a browser tab so it's easier to see — opening it now at <URL>. (It's token-intensive, so say the word if you'd rather keep things in the terminal.)"
282	
283	If a visual question never arises, never open it. If the user asks to stop using it, continue text-only and don't reopen it unless they raise it again.
284	
285	**Per-question decision:** Even with the companion open, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**
286	
287	- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
288	- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions
289	
290	A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.
291	
292	Before opening the companion for the first time, read the detailed guide:
293	`skills/brainstorming/visual-companion.md`
294	
295	## After the Design (architectural path)
296	
297	**Documentation:**
298	
299	- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/hyperpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
300	  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
301	- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
302	- Do NOT commit the design document. Leave it as an uncommitted working file unless the user explicitly asks you to commit it.
303	- Where the design rests on something nobody confirmed, write it as
304	  `Assumption: <what>, validate via <method>` rather than as a fact; the
305	  plan will attach the deadline. The placeholder scan accepts that form
306	  and flags bare TBD or TODO.
307	
308	**Spec Self-Review:**
309	After writing the spec document, look at it with fresh eyes:
310	
311	1. **Placeholder scan:** Any "TBD", "TODO", incomplete sections, or vague requirements? Fix them.
312	2. **Internal consistency:** Do any sections contradict each other? Does the architecture match the feature descriptions?
313	3. **Scope check:** Is this focused enough for a single implementation plan, or does it need decomposition?
314	4. **Ambiguity check:** Could any requirement be interpreted two different ways? If so, pick one and make it explicit.
315	
316	Fix any issues inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on.
317	
318	**Codex Spec Review Gate (Claude Code only):**
319	After the spec self-review passes and before involving the user, run the Codex
320	review gate over the spec file as a **document** review using the spec recipe.
321	Follow
322	[../requesting-code-review/codex-review-gate.md](../requesting-code-review/codex-review-gate.md):
323	probe availability, and if Codex is present, provide the spec path plus any
324	available approved-design context, have it review the spec, and resolve blocking
325	findings in the convergence fix loop (document-gate backstop of 4 rounds) before
326	the user review; if Codex is absent, emit the no-Codex notice and proceed. This
327	gate never blocks the user review — at worst it is skipped.
328	
329	**User Review Gate:**
330	After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:
331	
332	> "Spec written to `<path>` (not committed). Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."
333	
334	Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.
335	
336	**Implementation:**
337	
338	- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
339	- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.

2	name: brainstorming
3	description: "You MUST use this before any creative work - creating features, building components, adding functionality, or modifying behavior. Explores user intent, requirements and design before implementation."
4	---
5	
6	# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs
7	
8	Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.
9	
10	Start by classifying how much process the request needs, then work
11	through your path: understand the context, refine the idea, present a
12	design, and get your human partner's approval.
13	
14	<HARD-GATE>
15	Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any
16	project, or take any implementation action until you have told your
17	human partner what you intend and they have approved it. This applies
18	to EVERY task on EVERY path below — the ceremony scales with the task;
19	the approval gate never does.
20	</HARD-GATE>
21	
22	**REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use hyperpowers:communication for everything your human partner reads on every path: the questions, the approach comparison, the design presentation, and the spec.
23	
24	**After every context compaction:** Claude Code re-attaches this skill cut to its first 20,000 characters, which ends before the spec-writing steps, and a full Read you made before the compaction does not survive it. After each compaction, the first and every later one, Read this file in full before your next action (a question to your human partner, a visual-companion step, or writing the spec), along with any other skill you are following whose re-attached copy is cut short.
25	
26	## Three Paths
27	
28	Before your first question, classify the request and say the
29	classification out loud — "this looks bounded, so I'll present a short
30	design here rather than write a spec" — so your human partner can
31	override it:
32	
33	- **Spike** — a feasibility question ("can we...", "is it possible...",
34	  "quick and dirty is fine") whose output is an answer, not code you
35	  keep. Present the question and what you'll try in 2-3 sentences, get
36	  a nod, then find out as cheaply as correctness allows. No design
37	  doc, no spec file. Report findings as a recommendation; anything you
38	  built stays labeled throwaway.
39	- **Bounded** — a well-scoped change to code that already exists in
40	  this repo: a new flag, a small endpoint, a one-file fix.
41	  Understanding the kind of app is not enough — bounded means the flow
42	  you are changing is already here to read. If there is no existing
43	  flow to change, the task is not bounded. Classify by the outcome the
44	  request names, not by the code your first edit would touch: if the
45	  request names structure this repo does not have — a new module or
46	  layer, a new subsystem such as logging or storage, reuse across
47	  components that do not exist yet — the flow you would be changing is
48	  not already here, however small the first edit looks, and the task
49	  is architectural. Choosing between algorithms or options inside a
50	  function that already exists names no new structure and stays
51	  bounded. Ask the clarifying questions that matter, present a short
52	  design IN CHAT (a few sentences to a few short paragraphs), and
53	  STOP. Implementation starts only after your human partner says yes
54	  to that design — a bounded task's approval is as hard a gate as an
55	  architectural one. No spec file, no implementation plan document.
56	- **Architectural** — new projects, new subsystems, changes that
57	  restructure how components fit together or alter interfaces others
58	  depend on. Follow the full process: questions, approaches, sectioned
59	  design, written spec, then the writing-plans skill.
60	
61	When in doubt between two paths, take the heavier one. The ratchet is
62	one-way: hidden complexity discovered mid-task upgrades the path —
63	stop, say so, and step up. Nothing downgrades mid-task.
64	
65	## Anti-Pattern: "Too Simple To Need Approval"
66	
67	Every path ends with your human partner approving your intent before
68	implementation. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config
69	change — the design may be two sentences in chat, but you MUST present
70	it and get approval. "Simple" tasks are where unexamined assumptions
71	cause the most wasted work. What scales with simplicity is the
72	artifact, never the approval.
73	
74	## Red Flags
75	
76	| Thought | Reality |
77	|---------|---------|
78	| "This is too simple to need a design" | Simple means a short design, not no design. Two sentences in chat, then approval. |
79	| "I'll call it bounded and skip the spec" | Reaching for a label to skip work IS the doubt — take the heavier path. |
80	| "It's bounded and the design is obvious — I'll start while they read it" | The gate is the approval, not the design's length. Present, then stop until you hear yes. |
81	| "I understand this kind of app, so it's bounded" | Bounded measures the repo, not your familiarity. A new project has no existing flow — it is architectural. |
82	| "The code I'd touch is right here, so it's bounded" | Bounded measures the outcome's shape, not the entry point. A request naming a new module, a new subsystem, or reuse across components that do not exist yet is architectural even when the edit starts in one file. |
83	| "The spike works, so I'll keep the code" | A spike's output is an answer. Keeping the code is a new request — classify it. |
84	| "It grew, but I'm almost done — no need to re-classify" | Hidden complexity upgrades the path mid-task. Stop and say so. |
85	| "They approved the spike, so the follow-up change is approved too" | Each task gets its own classification and its own approval. |
86	| "It's bounded, so the visual companion doesn't apply" | The companion keys on the question being visual, not on the path being heavy. Open it — the task stays bounded. |

211	**Understanding the idea:**
212	
213	- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
214	- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
215	- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
216	- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
217	- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too. When the options differ in what happens afterward, the comparison goes in chat before you ask — see Deciding Together below
218	- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
219	- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria
220	
221	**Exploring approaches:**
222	
223	- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
224	- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
225	- Lead with your recommended option and explain why
226	- YAGNI ruthlessly - remove unnecessary features from every approach and design
227	- **Codex approach gate (conditional):** when the design space has real architectural, algorithmic, or data-model alternatives — or your human partner explicitly asks — get Codex's independent approaches first via [codex-approach-gate.md](codex-approach-gate.md): blind handoff, one shot, approaches folded into this step with provenance tags and judged on merits, not origin.
228	
229	**Presenting the design:**
230	
231	- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
232	- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
233	- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
234	- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
235	- For a new project (or one with no configured tooling), the design presentation includes a short tooling question alongside the architecture: which of these to set up from the start — cheapest before any code exists: aggressive linting + auto-formatting (the stack's standard, e.g. ruff+format / eslint+prettier / clippy+rustfmt); unit-test infrastructure (runner, layout, a first passing fixture); end-to-end test infrastructure; fuzz or mutation testing where the stack supports it. The user's selections land in the spec's Global Constraints so every later plan and task inherits them.
236	- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense
237	
238	**Design for isolation and clarity:**
239	
240	- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
241	- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
242	- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
243	- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.
244	
245	**Working in existing codebases:**
246	
247	- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
248	- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
249	- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.
250	
251	## Deciding Together
252	
253	Five-word labels with a line of description each are plenty for "which of
254	these do you prefer" and nowhere near enough for a choice your human partner
255	has to live with. Whenever the options differ in what happens afterward — an
256	interface, a stored format, a default, a dependency, work that would have to
257	be redone — the comparison goes in chat, before you ask.
258	
259	That message has three parts, in this order:
260	
261	1. **The fork**, in one sentence: what actually differs between the options,
262	   not what they are named.
263	2. **One line per option**: what it buys, what it costs, and what it rules
264	   out later. Say which choices are cheap to change afterward and which are
265	   not.
266	3. **Your recommendation**, and the reason you hold it.
267	
268	Send that message. Then ask with the normal selection widget — short labels,
269	one line of description each, your recommended option first. The message is
270	how they decide; the widget is how they answer. You send both, and you fold
271	neither into the other.
272	
273	If the options differ only in what they are called — a name, an ordering, a
274	wording — ask directly. There is nothing to compare.
275	
276	## Visual Companion
277	
278	A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode, and not a path. Having it open means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.
279	
280	**Using the companion (just-in-time):** Do NOT open it upfront. Wait until a question would genuinely be clearer shown than told — a real mockup / layout / diagram question, not merely a UI *topic*. The first time that happens, just use it: start the server with `--open` so the user's browser opens to the first screen, and tell them what you're doing in the same message — no separate approval gate.
281	> "I'll sketch this in a browser tab so it's easier to see — opening it now at <URL>. (It's token-intensive, so say the word if you'd rather keep things in the terminal.)"
282	
283	If a visual question never arises, never open it. If the user asks to stop using it, continue text-only and don't reopen it unless they raise it again.
284	
285	**Per-question decision:** Even with the companion open, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**
286	
287	- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
288	- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions
289	
290	A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.
291	
292	Before opening the companion for the first time, read the detailed guide:
293	`skills/brainstorming/visual-companion.md`
294	
295	## After the Design (architectural path)
296	
297	**Documentation:**
298	
299	- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/hyperpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
300	  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
301	- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
302	- Do NOT commit the design document. Leave it as an uncommitted working file unless the user explicitly asks you to commit it.
303	- Where the design rests on something nobody confirmed, write it as
304	  `Assumption: <what>, validate via <method>` rather than as a fact; the
305	  plan will attach the deadline. The placeholder scan accepts that form
306	  and flags bare TBD or TODO.
307	
308	**Spec Self-Review:**
309	After writing the spec document, look at it with fresh eyes:
310	
311	1. **Placeholder scan:** Any "TBD", "TODO", incomplete sections, or vague requirements? Fix them.
312	2. **Internal consistency:** Do any sections contradict each other? Does the architecture match the feature descriptions?
313	3. **Scope check:** Is this focused enough for a single implementation plan, or does it need decomposition?
314	4. **Ambiguity check:** Could any requirement be interpreted two different ways? If so, pick one and make it explicit.
315	
316	Fix any issues inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on.
317	
318	**Codex Spec Review Gate (Claude Code only):**
319	After the spec self-review passes and before involving the user, run the Codex
320	review gate over the spec file as a **document** review using the spec recipe.
321	Follow
322	[../requesting-code-review/codex-review-gate.md](../requesting-code-review/codex-review-gate.md):
323	probe availability, and if Codex is present, provide the spec path plus any
324	available approved-design context, have it review the spec, and resolve blocking
325	findings in the convergence fix loop (document-gate backstop of 4 rounds) before
326	the user review; if Codex is absent, emit the no-Codex notice and proceed. This
327	gate never blocks the user review — at worst it is skipped.
328	
329	**User Review Gate:**
330	After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:
331	
332	> "Spec written to `<path>` (not committed). Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."
333	
334	Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.
335	
336	**Implementation:**
337	
338	- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
339	- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.
340
